claim: Eurasian common shrews (Sorex araneus) endure winter by shrinking their brain, skull, and most organs, only to then regrow to breeding size the following spring.
source: Contrasting almost all other mammalian wintering strategies, Eurasian common shrews, Sorex araneus, endure winter by shrinking their brain, skull, and most organs, only to then regrow to breeding size the following spring.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on Dehnel's phenomenon in shrews.

claim: The common shrew loses up to 18% body mass, ~20% skull volume, and 26% brain mass during winter shrinkage.
source: In the most acute case of Dehnel's phenomenon, or seasonal size plasticity, the common shrew first grows to an initial summer maximum as a juvenile, then shrinks in autumn losing up to 18% body mass, ~20% skull volume, and 26% brain mass, reaching its winter size minimum (Lázaro et al., 2019; Pucek, 1970; Pucek, 1965b; Pucek, 1965a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting these measurements.

claim: Dehnel's phenomenon is hypothesized to be an adaptation to decrease energy demand without slowing metabolism through plasticity.
source: Dehnel's phenomenon is hypothesized to be an adaptation to decrease energy demand without slowing metabolism through plasticity, improving shrew fitness during the low temperatures and limited food supply of winter (Lázaro et al., 2019; Pucek, 1970; Pucek, 1965a; Keicher et al., 2017; Churchfield et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2013; Hyvärinen, 1984; Schaeffer et al., 2020; Thomas et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies proposing this adaptive hypothesis.

claim: Dehnel's phenomenon anticipates winter conditions and is both geographically variable and modulated by environmental temperature.
source: Corroborating this adaptive plasticity hypothesis, Dehnel's phenomenon anticipates winter conditions and is both geographically variable (Pucek, 1970) and modulated by environmental temperature (Lázaro et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating geographic variation and temperature modulation.

claim: Sorex araneus has one of the highest basal metabolic rates per unit of body mass identified in any mammal.
source: Compared to most species, S. araneus has astronomically large energy demands, with one the highest basal metabolic rates per unit of body mass identified in any mammal (Genoud et al., 2018; Taylor, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies measuring metabolic rates.

claim: Sorex araneus forage and feed constantly to meet their energy requirements.
source: To meet these energy requirements, S. araneus forage and feed constantly.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the high metabolic rate and established knowledge of shrew behavior.

claim: Sorex araneus have brief lifespans of approximately 1 year that require surviving a single winter.
source: Together with brief lifespans (~1 year) that nonetheless require surviving a single winter (Searle et al., 2019; Healy et al., 2014), these extreme metabolic demands constrain survival options for S. araneus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting shrew lifespans.

claim: The hypothalamus undergoes a 31.6% volume reduction in autumn through winter in shrews.
source: In shrews, the hypothalamus undergoes a 31.6% volume reduction in autumn through winter, followed by a 47.8% increase in spring (Lázaro et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study measuring hypothalamus volume changes.

claim: The hypothalamus undergoes a 47.8% volume increase in spring in shrews.
source: In shrews, the hypothalamus undergoes a 31.6% volume reduction in autumn through winter, followed by a 47.8% increase in spring (Lázaro et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study measuring hypothalamus volume changes.

claim: The hypothalamus plays a pivotal role in the maintenance of energy budgets across all mammals.
source: Across all mammals, the hypothalamus plays a pivotal role in the maintenance of energy budgets, with functions influencing: (1) energy intake and feeding behavior, (2) energy expenditure and metabolic rate, and (3) energy deficits and storage.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about hypothalamic function.

claim: 786 of 19,296 genes passed filters for temporal variation in hypothalamus gene expression (>0.5-fold change between any two seasons and 2 samples>10 normalized reads).
source: Most genes did not exhibit much variation through time, indicating constitutive gene expression in the hypothalamus, as only 786 of 19,296 genes passed our filters (>0.5-fold change between any two seasons and 2 samples>10 normalized reads).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results from the study.

claim: 12 distinct clusters of gene expression patterns were identified by bootstrapping a gap statistic within cluster distances.
source: We identified 12 distinct clusters of gene expression patterns by bootstrapping (n=20) a gap statistic within cluster distances.
evidence: The claim is supported by the clustering analysis performed in the study.

claim: Five clusters consisting of 392 genes resembled a large divergence between summer juveniles and the remaining individuals without a second local maximum during size change.
source: Of these 12 clusters, five clusters consisting of 392 genes resembled a large divergence between summer juveniles and the remaining individuals without a second local maximum during size change (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Clusters 2, 3, 8, 11, 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and reference to a figure showing the clusters.

claim: 392 genes likely represent a large developmental shift between recently postnatal shrews and the remainder of individuals compared to shifts associated with seasonality or Dehnel's phenomenon.
source: These genes likely represent a large developmental shift between recently postnatal shrews and the remainder of individuals compared to shifts associated with seasonality or Dehnel's phenomenon.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the clustering pattern observed.

claim: 14 pathways were enriched prior to Bonferroni correction (p<0.05; modified Fisher's exact test) in the functional characterization of 394 seasonally varying genes.
source: Although no enrichment pathway was significant after a Bonferroni correction, 14 pathways were enriched prior to correction (p<0.05; modified Fisher's exact test), with the five pathways with the lowest p-values including fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis, relaxin signaling, neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, HIF-1 signaling, and phosphoinositide-3 kinase (PI3K)-Akt signaling (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis results shown in the figure.

claim: 210 differentially expressed genes were found between autumn and spring shrews, with 129 upregulated and 81 downregulated in spring.
source: By comparing the RNA expression of autumn and spring shrews, we found 210 DEGs, with 129 upregulated and 81 downregulated in spring (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis results shown in the figure.

claim: 15 pathways were enriched (p<0.05; modified Fisher's exact test) with significant genes prior to multiple comparison correction in the functional characterization of 210 DEGs in the hypothalamus.
source: We ran a GO pathway enrichment to functionally characterize the 210 DEGs in the hypothalamus and found 15 pathways were enriched (p<0.05; modified Fisher's exact test) with significant genes prior to multiple comparison correction.
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis results.

claim: All enriched pathways in the hypothalamus DEG analysis were downregulated in spring.
source: These pathways were all downregulated in spring and included pathways in cancer (4.5-fold enrichment, p<0.001), transcriptional misregulation in cancer (8.3-fold enrichment, p<0.001), fluid shear stress and atherosclerosis (9.5-fold enrichment, p<0.01), small cell lung cancer (11.5-fold enrichment, p<0.01), IL-17 signaling (11.3-fold enrichment, p<0.01), cAMP signaling (5.9-fold enrichment, p<0.01), and apoptosis (7.8-fold enrichment, p<0.05) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis results shown in the figure.

claim: Pathways in cancer consisted of nine significantly downregulated genes, four of which overlapped with apoptotic pathways including BCL2L1, NFKBIA, FOS, and GADD45B.
source: Pathways in cancer consisted of nine significantly downregulated genes (from DESeq2 Wald test), four of which overlapped with apoptotic pathways including BCL2L1 (–0.6 log-fold change [LFC] padj<0.01), NFKBIA (–1.3 LFC, padj<0.01), FOS (–1.5 LFC, padj<0.05), and GADD45B (–1.4 LFC, padj<0.05) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis results shown in the figure.

claim: Heat significantly reduced cell viability compared to controls in MPF neural cell lines.
source: A significant difference in cell viability was observed between the heat scrambled compared to the control scrambled groups (df = 3.56, t3.56=8.78, p<0.01), however, there was no significant difference between cells transfected with BCL2L1 compared to those transfected with sBCL2L1 when exposed to heat (df = 3.37, t3.37=-0.99, p=0.39).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays.

claim: BCL2L1 overexpression did not rescue heat-induced reduction in cell viability in MPF neural cell lines.
source: A significant difference in cell viability was observed between the heat scrambled compared to the control scrambled groups (df = 3.56, t3.56=8.78, p<0.01), however, there was no significant difference between cells transfected with BCL2L1 compared to those transfected with sBCL2L1 when exposed to heat (df = 3.37, t3.37=-0.99, p=0.39).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays.

claim: 222 genes significantly rejected a single expression optimum for all species in favor of a second expression optimum for the shrew lineage (padj<0.05).
source: Expression variance and evolution (EVE) models found 222 genes significantly rejected (padj<0.05) a single expression optimum for all species in favor of a second expression optimum for the shrew lineage.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic comparative analysis results.

claim: All second optima in the shrew lineage were higher than the first optimum in the EVE model analysis.
source: Notably, all second optima (in the shrew lineage) were higher than the first optimum, consistent with results from the original methods manuscript (Rohlfs et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic comparative analysis results and citation to the methods paper.

claim: Genes experiencing an expression branch-shift in shrews had a mean 9.66 orthologous transcripts per million (oTPM)-fold change compared to other species.
source: While nonsignificant genes had a mean 0.93-fold change, genes experiencing an expression branch-shift in shrews had a mean 9.66 orthologous transcripts per million (oTPM)-fold change compared to other species.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative gene expression analysis results.

claim: 81 genes had significantly lower β (within population variance to between-species variance) in the dropout test, suggesting selection elsewhere in the phylogeny.
source: Of the 6496 genes tested, 81 genes had significantly (padj<0.05) lower β (within population variance to between-species variance), suggesting selection elsewhere in the phylogeny.
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic comparative analysis results.

claim: None of the 81 genes with selection elsewhere in the phylogeny overlapped with those identified to be differentially expressed in the shrew.
source: None of these genes overlapped with those identified to be differentially expressed in the shrew, further validating the specificity of expression shifts.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of results from different analyses.

claim: Two significantly enriched pathways were identified in genes with shrew-specific upregulation: calcium signaling (2.8-fold enrichment, p<0.05) and autophagy (9.1-fold enrichment, p<0.05).
source: Pathway enrichment analysis identified two significantly enriched pathways: calcium signaling (2.8-fold enrichment, p<0.05) and autophagy (9.1-fold enrichment, p<0.05) (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis results shown in the figure.

claim: Four genes overlap between those experiencing branch-shift changes in expression and those differentially expressed between autumn and spring individuals: CCDC22, LMX1A, KCNS1, and PAQR4.
source: Four of the genes experiencing branch-shift changes in expression were also differentially expressed between autumn and spring individuals, suggesting not only an adaptive shift in the shrew lineage associated with the evolution of Dehnel's phenomenon, but also a direct molecular mechanism for brain changes. The four genes that overlap between both analyses include Figure 4: CCDC22, which plays an important role in endosomal recycling of membrane proteins (Singla et al., 2019); LMX1A, a transcription factor essential for dopaminergic neuron development Hoekstra et al., 2013; KCNS1, which encodes a subunit of potassium channels associated with neuronal excitability and pain sensitivity Tsantoulas et al., 2018; and PAQR4, which appears to regulate growth and apoptosis through sphingolipid synthesis in human cancers (Pedersen et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of results from different analyses and citations to studies describing gene functions.

claim: Identifying four overlapping genes is not significantly greater than expected by chance (Fisher's exact test, p=0.55).
source: However, identifying four overlapping genes is not significantly greater than expected by chance (Fisher's exact test, p=0.55).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing of the overlap.

claim: Relaxin-3 is upregulated by food restriction in vivo.
source: food restriction upregulates relaxin-3 (RLN3) in vivo (Lenglos et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this effect.

claim: Administering RLN3 protein into the rat hypothalamus vastly increases food intake.
source: while administering RLN3 protein into the rat hypothalamus vastly increases food intake (de Ávila et al., 2018; Calvez et al., 2015; Lenglos et al., 2015; McGowan et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this effect.

claim: Relaxin activates the PI3K pathway.
source: Relaxin has also been found to activate the PI3K pathway (Ahmad et al., 2012; Dessauer and Nguyen, 2005)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this activation.

claim: PI3K pathway mediates feeding behavior and glucose homeostasis.
source: which mediates feeding behavior and glucose homeostasis (Shen et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2017; Niswender et al., 2001; Könner et al., 2007; Hill et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these functions.

claim: PI3K pathway mediates angiogenesis via vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) production.
source: as well as angiogenesis via vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) production (Dessauer and Nguyen, 2005; Karar and Maity, 2011; Maity et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this function.

claim: Neural progenitor cells and surrounding astro- and pericytes express VEGFA and WNT7A defining an expression gradient that guides blood vessels to form the BBB in normal neural development.
source: In normal neural development, neural progenitor cells and surrounding astro- and pericytes express these two genes defining an expression gradient that guides blood vessels to form the BBB (Raab et al., 2004; Carmeliet et al., 1996; Daneman et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this developmental process.

claim: Continued expression of VEGFA beyond development increases BBB permeability, leading to a breakdown of its protective effects.
source: While this suggests VEGFA and WNT7A upregulation in the shrew may increase vascularization of the brain, continued expression of VEGFA beyond development increases BBB permeability, leading to a breakdown of its protective effects (Argaw et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this effect.

claim: BBB permeability is a common symptom of many disease-like states including neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration.
source: BBB permeability is a common symptom of many disease-like states including neuroinflammation (Argaw et al., 2009) and neurodegeneration (Argaw et al., 2009; Lan et al., 2022; Obermeier et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this association.

claim: Reduced blood glucose levels from fasting promote capillary fenestration in the hypothalamic BBB via upregulation of VEGFA in mice.
source: Experiments on mice indicate reduced blood glucose levels from fasting promote capillary fenestration in the hypothalamic BBB via upregulation of VEGFA, eliciting feeding responses through increased hypothalamic exposure to glucose levels (Langlet et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this mechanism in mice.

claim: Upregulation of VEGFA and WNT7A in shrews may constitutively increase capillary fenestration, a potential adaptation of the BBB to improve hypothalamus metabolic sensing and signaling in response to high energy demands.
source: In shrews, upregulation of VEGFA and WNT7A may constitutively increase capillary fenestration, a potential adaptation of the BBB to improve hypothalamus metabolic sensing and signaling in response to high energy demands.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed gene expression patterns and known functions of these genes.

claim: Adaptive expression of VEGFA has been identified in the seasonal vascular plasticity of reproductive sheep, bison, and squirrels.
source: Notably, adaptive expression of VEGFA has also been identified in the seasonal vascular plasticity of other mammal species, including reproductive sheep (Chevillard et al., 2022; Castle-Miller et al., 2017), bison (Tabecka-Lonczynska et al., 2018), and squirrels (Yao et al., 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating VEGFA expression in other species.

claim: In the hypothalamus, FOXO1 negatively regulates POMC and promotes AgRP expression.
source: For example, in the hypothalamus FOXO1 negatively regulates POMC and promotes AgRP expression (Ma et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this regulatory relationship.

claim: FOXO1 can contribute to leptin resistance resulting in long-term appetite suppression.
source: which can contribute to leptin resistance resulting in a long-term appetite suppression (Amitani et al., 2013; Sasaki et al., 2010; Nakae et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this effect.

claim: In mouse adipocytes, leptin-dependent expression of FOXO4 can rapidly clear blood glucose levels.
source: In mouse adipocytes, leptin-dependent expression of FOXO4 can rapidly clear blood glucose levels (Wang et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this effect in mice.

claim: Upregulation of FOXO4 in shrews could either increase blood glucose clearance or leptin resistance, reducing long-term satiation and promoting continuous feeding.
source: We hypothesize that, in shrews, upregulation of FOXO4 could either increase blood glucose clearance or leptin resistance, reducing long-term satiation and promoting continuous feeding.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the potential effects of FOXO4 upregulation in shrews.

claim: Shrews show no reduction in cell number despite seasonal decreases in brain mass and volume.
source: Progressive cell loss in neurons is a hallmark of neurodegeneration (Wilson et al., 2023), but despite seasonal decreases in brain mass and volume, shrews show no reduction in cell number (Smith, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this observation.

claim: BCL2L1 promotes cell survival by reducing apoptosis through an NFKB-dependent pathway in rodents.
source: As a known anti-apoptotic gene, BCL2L1 promotes cell survival by reducing apoptosis through an NFKB-dependent pathway, as demonstrated in rodents (Bui et al., 2001; Motoyama et al., 1995; Boise and Thompson, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism in rodents.

claim: The BCL2 gene family is recognized for its contrasting roles in disease, with upregulation in CNS disorders and downregulation in cancers.
source: The BCL2 gene family is also recognized for its contrasting roles in disease, with upregulation in CNS disorders and downregulation in cancers.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about BCL2 family genes in disease.

claim: Natural experiments in hibernators found seasonal reduction of apoptosis, paired with upregulation of BCL2L1.
source: For example, natural experiments in hibernators found seasonal reduction of apoptosis, paired with upregulation of BCL2L1 (Fleck and Carey, 2005; Logan et al., 2016), including in the brain (Rouble et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this pattern in hibernators.

claim: MLST8 is an integral component of the mTOR protein complex 1 (mTORC1) that regulates sugar and lipid metabolism.
source: This included MLST8, an integral component of the mTOR protein complex 1 (mTORC1) that regulates sugar and lipid metabolism (Guertin et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study describing MLST8 function.

claim: MLST8 has been found to modulate autophagy in response to nutrient deprivation.
source: but also has recently been found to modulate autophagy in response to nutrient deprivation (Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this function.

claim: PPIF is an important component of the mitochondrial permeability transition, which responds to cellular calcium overload and oxidative stress by promoting cell death.
source: PPIF is an important component of the mitochondrial permeability transition, which responds to cellular calcium overload and oxidative stress by promoting cell death (Baines et al., 2005; Nakagawa et al., 2005; Li et al., 2009; Halestrap, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing PPIF function.

claim: Overexpression of SPHK2 in stressed cells induces cell cycle arrest and promotes apoptosis through a series of signaling cascades that increase cytosolic calcium and promote the release of pro-apoptotic cytochrome c from the mitochondria.
source: Similar to PPIF, overexpression of SPHK2 in stressed cells induces cell cycle arrest and promotes apoptosis through a series of signaling cascades that increase cytosolic calcium and promote the release of pro-apoptotic cytochrome c from the mitochondria (Maceyka et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this mechanism.

claim: SPHK2 and PPIF are overexpressed and likely contribute to neuronal death in both human patients with Huntington's disease or Alzheimer's disease and rodent models of these diseases.
source: While both SPHK2 and PPIF are overexpressed and likely contribute to neuronal death in both human patients with Huntington's disease or Alzheimer's disease and rodent models of these diseases
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature on these genes in neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Knockout or inhibition of SPHK2 and PPIF protects against neurodegeneration.
source: knockout or inhibition of these genes protects against neurodegeneration (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2017; Takasugi et al., 2011; Du et al., 2008; Du et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this protective effect.

claim: CCDC22 plays a key role in endosomal recycling of proteins and is a novel candidate gene for several neurological disorders.
source: The coiled-coil domain containing 22 protein (CCDC22) plays a key role in endosomal recycling of proteins and is a novel candidate gene for several neurological disorders (Voineagu et al., 2012; Kolanczyk et al., 2015; Neri et al., 2022; Gjerulfsen et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing CCDC22 function and disease associations.

claim: CCDC22 is a subunit of the CCC (CCDC22, CCDC93, COMMD) complex that aids in trafficking and recycling of endosomal membrane proteins.
source: CCDC22 is a subunit of the CCC (CCDC22, CCDC93, COMMD) complex that aids in trafficking and recycling of endosomal membrane proteins (Singla et al., 2019; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Bartuzi et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing the CCC complex function.

claim: Improper recycling and resulting protein aggregation readily occurs in neurons, as they do not proliferate.
source: Improper recycling and resulting protein aggregation readily occurs in neurons, as they do not proliferate (Rubinsztein, 2006; McDonald, 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies describing this phenomenon in neurons.

claim: Protein aggregation has been implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, including cytotoxicity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, amyloid-B aggregation in Alzheimer's disease, and MUL1 degradation in Parkinson's disease.
source: and has also been implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, including cytotoxicity in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Muzio et al., 2020), amyloid-B aggregation in Alzheimer's disease (Small et al., 2005; Rogaeva et al., 2007; Lane et al., 2010), and MUL1 degradation in Parkinson's disease (Tang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these disease associations.

claim: Missense mutations and subsequent downregulation of CCDC22 are potential mechanisms underlying X-linked intellectual disability and Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome in humans.
source: Missense mutations and subsequent downregulation of CCDC22 are potential mechanisms underlying X-linked intellectual disability (Voineagu et al., 2012; Kolanczyk et al., 2015) and Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome (Kolanczyk et al., 2015; Neri et al., 2022; Gjerulfsen et al., 2021) in humans.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating these disease associations.

claim: X-linked intellectual disability and Ritscher-Schinzel syndrome are characterized by macrocephaly, malformations of the brain, craniofacial abnormalities, and intellectual disabilities.
source: Both disorders are characterized by macrocephaly, malformations of the brain, craniofacial abnormalities, and intellectual disabilities.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about these disorders.

claim: CCDC22 has an ~7-fold upregulation in pubescent spring shrews compared to other mammals.
source: In pubescent spring shrews, we found CCDC22 has an ~7-fold upregulation compared to other mammals and a significant upregulation during spring compared to autumn shrinkage.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative gene expression analysis results.

claim: CCDC22 has a significant upregulation during spring compared to autumn shrinkage in shrews.
source: In pubescent spring shrews, we found CCDC22 has an ~7-fold upregulation compared to other mammals and a significant upregulation during spring compared to autumn shrinkage.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis results.

claim: Sorex araneus were collected from a single German population (47.9684 N, 8.9761 E) across five different seasons of Dehnel's phenomenon from June 2020 to June 2021 (n=25, nper_season = 4–5).
source: Briefly, S. araneus were collected from a single German population (47.9684 N, 8.9761 E) across five different seasons of Dehnel's phenomenon from June 2020 to June 2021 (n=25, nper_season = 4–5, protocols authorized by Regierungspräsidium Freiburg, Baden-Württemberg 35-9185.81/G-19/131).
evidence: The claim describes the sample collection methodology.

claim: Hypothalamus libraries were prepared with poly-A selection and sequenced for approximately 15–25 million reads per sample in 150 bp PE reads.
source: Hypothalamus libraries were prepared with poly-A selection and sequenced for approximately 15–25 million reads per sample in 150 bp PE reads.
evidence: The claim describes the sequencing methodology.

claim: 6496 single-copy orthologs were retained across all species for comparative analysis.
source: Orthologous genes between species were inferred with OrthoFinder (Emms and Kelly, 2019) using default parameters, retaining only single-copy orthologs identified across all species (n=6496 single-copy orthologs).
evidence: The claim describes the orthology inference results.
